Convex Lens Imaging · Move the Candle, Change the Image

A candle stands before a convex lens: far away, its image is small and upside-down; drag it closer and the image grows; drag it past one special point and the image suddenly jumps to the same side of the lens, upright and magnified. No magic — just two watershed points: one focal length splits real from virtual, two focal lengths split shrinking from magnifying. Every image on this page is computed live from the lens formula 1/f = 1/u + 1/v — what the picture shows and what the words say are the same image.

Step 0 · Light through a Lens

Parallel light goes in — the lens gathers it to one point

Known: light travels straight in one medium and bends at an interface (refraction). This step answers one question only: where does a bundle of parallel light go after passing through a convex lens? Two names first: the straight line through the centre of the lens, perpendicular to it, is the principal axis; the centre point of the lens is the optical centre O. Drag the focal-length slider and watch where the rays on the right meet.

Focal length f (focus to optical centre) 60

The parallel light is gathered onto one point of the axis — the focus F: it sits 60 to the right of the optical centre (that distance is the focal length); the 2F point sits at 120. With f = 60: a middling focal length gathers them unhurriedly.

Conclusion: a convex lens is a converging lens — it gathers parallel light to its focus. Conditions: this page draws the idealised case of a thin lens and rays near the axis; rays near the rim of a real lens deviate slightly (spherical aberration), which this page does not develop.

Step 1 · Three Special Rays

Locating one image point takes only three rays

This step answers: the flame tip emits countless rays — how do we know where its image lands? Trick: draw only three rays with rules — after the lens they are bound to meet again at the image point. You can drag the flame tip (up/down changes the height, left/right the object distance) or use the sliders below. Light the three rays one by one and watch where they meet. Here f = 60, and the image distance is not measured with a ruler — the formula computes it: 1/f = 1/u + 1/v.

Ray 1 · Parallel → through focus
Ray 2 · Through centre → straight
Ray 3 · Through focus → parallel
Object distance u (candle to centre) 120
Object height (flame tip to axis) 30

Ray 1: leaves parallel to the axis, bends at the lens toward the far focus F.

Object distance u = 120; the formula gives image distance v = 120. The lit rays meet exactly there: image height 30 (1× the object height 30, inverted). Any two rays fix the point — the third joins on its own.

Conclusion: these three rays are the whole drawing method. A handy self-check: pick any two rays to fix the meeting point — the third must pass through it automatically. If it misses, the drawing is wrong.

Step 2 · Moving the Candle (the core step)

Drag the candle closer — the image wears five faces

This step answers one question: as the object distance u shrinks from large to small, how does the image change? Drag the candle (or use the slider and preset buttons) and watch the readout: orientation, size, real-or-virtual and image distance v are all computed live from the lens formula. Units first: distances are in “units”, f = 60; u is candle-to-centre, v is image-to-centre; F marks one focal length and 2F two focal lengths — the two watershed points.

● u>2f · smaller, real　● f<u<2f · bigger, real　● u<f · bigger, virtual

Object distance u 180
Far, 3f (u = 180)
Exactly 2f (u = 120)
Between f and 2f (u = 90)
Exactly f (u = 60)
Inside f (u = 30)

u = 180 (beyond 2f): the image sits on the other side, v = 90, magnification 0.5× — inverted, shrunk, real. A camera puts its subject in this zone.

Pocket rule: one focal length splits real from virtual; two focal lengths split small from large. Dragging in from far away, the image first grows (always inverted and real), and the moment it crosses F it jumps to the same side, upright and magnified. Conditions: convex lens, real object.

Step 3 · Screen and Eye

A real image can be caught; a virtual one can only be seen

This step answers: what really differs between a real and a virtual image? Scene one: the candle is fixed at u = 150 (f = 60), so the formula gives v = 100. Drag the screen to “catch” it — the flame on the screen is sharp only when the screen sits exactly at the image distance; move away and it blurs (the amount of blur here is drawn schematically from the defocus distance, not a true optical simulation). Scene two: move the candle inside f and see whether the screen can still catch anything — then use an eye instead.

Scene 1 · Catch a real image
Scene 2 · The magnifier’s virtual image
Screen position (distance from centre) 60

The screen is at 60; the image distance is 100, off by 40: the image blurs into a blob (blur drawn schematically). The rays have not met yet (or have met and spread again) — the screen only slices a patch of light. Drag it to 100 and try.

Conclusion: a real image is a true meeting of rays and can land on a screen; a virtual image is a meeting of backward extensions — eyes can see it, no screen ever catches it. A magnifying glass uses exactly a virtual image, which is why its letters cannot be projected onto paper.

Step 4 · Self-Test

Three questions on the two watersheds

No formulas — just the pocket rule: one focal length splits real from virtual, two split small from large. The axis diagram below stays available (f = 60).

Q1. A camera lens is a convex lens. The person stands far away (u > 2f). What is the image on the sensor like?

Inverted, smaller, real
Upright, magnified, virtual
Inverted, magnified, real

Tap an option to answer.

Q2. A candle is dragged slowly from 3f to 1.5f (staying outside f the whole way). How does the image change?

From magnified to smaller, still a real image
From smaller to magnified, still an inverted real image
Past some point it flips to an upright virtual image

Tap an option to answer.

Q3a. A projector needs an inverted, magnified, real image. Which zone should the slide be in?

u > 2f
f < u < 2f
u < f

Tap an option to answer.

Q3b. A magnifying glass needs an upright, magnified, virtual image. Which zone should the object be in?

u > 2f
f < u < 2f
u < f

Tap an option to answer.

All three questions ask the same thing: first locate u — beyond 2f, between f and 2f, or inside f — and orientation, size and real/virtual are all decided.

Step 5 · Finale

The whole page in three sentences

Same candle, same lens. Everything needed to predict the image is two watersheds plus three rays:

One focal length splits real from virtual

u > f: rays truly meet — a real image on the other side. u < f: only the backward extensions meet — a virtual image on the same side. u = f: the rays leave parallel, the image is at infinity.

Two focal lengths split small from large

u > 2f shrinks, u = 2f matches, f < u < 2f magnifies. Plus one blanket rule: real images are always inverted, virtual images always upright. Cameras, projectors and magnifiers merely park the object in different zones.

Three rays do the drawing

The parallel ray bends through the focus, the centre ray walks straight, the through-focus ray leaves parallel. Any two fix the image point; the third arrives on its own — and exposes a wrong drawing on the spot.

Starting from one bundle of parallel light, you can now predict the image at any distance: compute the image distance with 1/v = 1/f − 1/u, then compare u with f and 2f — orientation, size and real-vs-virtual all fall out. Cameras, projectors, magnifying glasses and the lens inside your own eye all run on this one formula.

Reflection & Refraction

Light travels straight inside one medium, but at a boundary it turns: it bounces off a mirror with the angle of reflection equal to the angle of incidence, bends as it enters water, and — at too steep an angle — reflects entirely back. Every ray on this page is computed from the real laws before it is drawn. Drag, measure, and see what light actually obeys.

中
EN
0 Mirror bounce
1 Diffuse reflection
2 Bending into water
3 Total reflection
4 The fooled eye

Step 0

Mirror bounce: angle in equals angle out

Question: when light hits a mirror, which way does it go? Two terms first: the normal is the imaginary line perpendicular to the mirror at the point of incidence (the dashed line in the diagram); the angle of incidence is measured between the incoming ray and the normal, and the angle of reflection between the reflected ray and the normal — both are measured from the normal, never from the mirror surface. Drag the light source in the diagram (or use the slider) and watch the two arc readings: however you drag, the angle of reflection always equals the angle of incidence. This holds for smooth, mirror-like surfaces.

Angle of incidence (or drag the source in the diagram)
Incidence 0° (head-on)
Incidence 60°
Reset this step

Angle of incidence = 35.0°, angle of reflection = 35.0° — equal.

Note: angles are measured from the normal. Measured from the mirror surface you would get 90° minus this value — textbooks always use the normal as the reference.

Step 1

Rough surfaces: diffuse reflection obeys the same law

Question: paper is not smooth, so why can we read it — yet never see our face in it? Zoomed in, a rough surface is a crowd of tiny facets tilted every which way, each with its own normal (the imaginary line perpendicular to that facet). A parallel beam lands on them; each ray still reflects with angle out equal to angle in at its own facet — this is diffuse reflection: the law does not fail; the normals point in different directions, so the reflected light scatters. Switch between the three views to compare.

Mirror
Rough surface
Side by side

Mirror: the normal points the same way everywhere, so parallel incoming rays stay parallel after reflecting — that is why a mirror forms a sharp image.

We can see non-luminous objects at all because diffuse reflection sends some of the light into our eyes from almost any viewing position.

Step 2

Bending into water: refraction turns toward the normal

Question: how does an oblique ray change angle when it enters water from air? The normal is perpendicular to the surface at the hit point. Incidence θ₁ and refraction θ₂ are measured from the normal on their respective sides. Drag the source or use the slider with the media fixed. At oblique incidence, the smaller refraction angle turns the ray toward the normal; at normal incidence both angles are0°. Expand the sine relation below to check this same ray.

Angle of incidence, air side (or drag the source)
Incidence 0° (straight in)
Reset this step

Angle of incidence = 40.0°, angle of refraction ≈ 28.9° (computed from Snell's law); the ray bent by 11.1° at the surface.

Refraction angle < incidence angle: entering water, the ray leans toward the normal.

The refractive index n=c/v is vacuum light speed c divided by the phase speed v in the medium; it is dimensionless. This ideal model fixes air at1.00 and water at1.33, with homogeneous, non-absorbing media and no dispersion. It computes ray directions, not travel times or reflected/transmitted energy fractions.

Math connection: can a real refraction angle exist?

Step 3

The other way: water to air, and total internal reflection

Question: when can light in water no longer propagate into air? Both angles are again measured from the normal, perpendicular to the surface. Below the critical angle, oblique rays bend away from the normal; at normal incidence both angles are0°. The incidence that gives refraction90°, the limiting ray along the surface, is the critical angle. Strictly above it, there is no propagating refracted ray in air: the ideal interface totally reflects the light inside water. Try30°, the exact critical preset and60°; predict whether a refracted ray exists before checking.

Incidence 30°
Critical preset (unrounded)≈48.8°
Incidence 60°
Reset this step

Angle of incidence = 30.0°, angle of refraction ≈ 41.7° — larger than the incidence angle; the ray leans away from the normal.

The critical angle is ≈ 48.8° (computed from arcsin(1/1.33)) — drag past it and see.

This critical angle requires higher incident index n₁ and lower exit index n₂: θc=arcsin(n₂/n₁). Here n₁=1.33 and n₂=1.00. The displayed48.8° is rounded; the preset uses the unrounded value. Arrow keys change0.1°; Home/End select0°/80°; dragging is continuous. Below critical, the faint orange ray is ordinary reflection. Line thickness and colour do not encode energy fractions.

Math connection: can a real refraction angle exist?

Step 4

The fooled eye: the fish is not where it looks

Question: how deep does the fish appear if we trace the ray reaching the eye backward? Light from the fish refracts at the water surface. This diagram extends the outgoing ray backward to the vertical reference line through the real fish and marks an apparent depth there. Move the eye or its slider to compare depths on that line. This explains a shallower appearance; it is not a full multi-ray virtual-image solution.

Eye position, left–right (or drag the eye in the diagram)

Real depth 3.5 units; it looks like only ≈2.3 units — the fish is lifted by about 1.2 units.

The apparent point stays on the vertical reference line through the fish; only depth is compared, not lateral image motion. Near the overhead, paraxial limit, apparent depth≈real depth/1.33. That ratio is not used at large viewing angles.

Quiz 1 · A ray hits a mirror at an incidence angle of 40°. What is the angle of reflection? (Measured from the normal.)
40°
50°
80°

Quiz 2 · Light enters water from air at 50°. The angle of refraction is —
smaller (bent toward the normal)
larger (bent away from the normal)
the same — no bend

Quiz 3 · A source under water shines at the surface with an incidence angle of 60° (critical angle ≈48.8°). What happens?
It refracts out, with a larger angle
The refracted ray skims along the surface
Total internal reflection — all of it reflects back

Quiz progress: not started yet.

Finale

Wrap-up: three rules at a boundary
Reflection: equal angles out

Angle of reflection = angle of incidence, both measured from the normal. The smoother the surface, the tidier the reflection; a rough surface only scrambles the normals, not the law.

Refraction: a new medium may change direction

Oblique air-to-water rays bend toward the normal; water-to-air rays bend away below critical. Normal incidence does not bend. Snell’s n₁sinθ₁=n₂sinθ₂ sets direction; n=c/v is dimensionless.

Virtual images: the eye looks back wrongly

The outgoing ray is extended backward to the fish’s vertical line to compare apparent depth. This reference-line illustration is not a full virtual-image solution.

See the atlas: unit circle → Snell and total reflection →

Why light slows down in water, and how convex lenses form images, belong to later pages; this page settles the accounts at the boundary itself.

一支蜡烛立在凸透镜前：离得远，像小而倒；拖近一点，像大起来；再拖过一个点，像忽然跳到镜子同一侧、正立放大。变的不是魔法，是两条分水岭：一倍焦距分虚实，二倍焦距分大小。这一页所有的像，都由透镜公式 1/f = 1/u + 1/v 当场算出来——图上画的、嘴里说的，必须是同一个像。

第 0 步 · 光穿过透镜

平行光进门，被透镜收拢到一点

已知：光在同一种介质里沿直线传播，穿过界面会拐弯（折射）。这一步只回答一个问题：一束互相平行的光穿过凸透镜，会往哪里走？先认两个名字：穿过透镜中心、且垂直于镜面的那条直线叫主光轴；透镜的中心点叫光心 O。拖动焦距滑杆，看右侧的光线交点怎样跟着移动。

焦距 f（焦点到光心的距离） 60

平行光被收拢到主光轴上的一点——这就是焦点 F：它在光心右侧 60 处（这段距离就叫焦距）；2F 点在 120 处。现在 f = 60：焦距中等，光线不慌不忙地收拢。

结论：凸透镜是会聚透镜——能把平行光会聚到焦点。适用条件：本页画的是薄透镜、靠近主光轴的光线这一理想情形；真实透镜靠边缘的光线会略有偏差（叫球差），本页不展开。

第 1 步 · 三条特殊光线

定位一个像点，只需要三条光线

这一步要回答：烛焰顶端这一点发出无数条光，怎么知道它的像落在哪里？办法是只画三条有规矩的光线——它们穿过透镜后必然在像点重新相会。烛焰顶端可以拖动（上下改物高、左右改物距），也可以用下面的滑杆。逐条点亮三条线，看它们在哪里相交。这里焦距 f = 60，像距不靠尺量、靠公式算：1/f = 1/u + 1/v。

线 1 · 平行→过焦点
线 2 · 过光心→不弯腰
线 3 · 过焦点→变平行
物距 u（蜡烛到光心） 28
物高（烛焰顶端到主光轴） 30

线 1：平行于主光轴出发，穿过透镜后拐向另一侧的焦点 F。

物距 u = 28（小于焦距 60）：右侧的光线是散开的、不相交；把它们反向延长（虚线），在左侧交出像点：像距 |v| = 52.5，像高 56.25（物高 30 的 ≈1.9 倍，正立）——这是虚像，第 3 步细说。

结论：作图定位像点就靠这三条线。检验自己画得对不对有个土办法：任意两条定交点，第三条必须自动穿过它——穿不过，就是画错了。

第 2 步 · 蜡烛远近（核心步）

蜡烛一路拖近，像连变五副面孔

这一步只回答一个问题：物距 u 从大到小一路变，像怎样跟着变？拖动蜡烛（或用滑杆、预设按钮），盯住下面的读数：像的正倒、大小、实虚、像距 v，全部由透镜公式当场算出。先认清单位与两个点：距离都以「单位」计，f = 60；物距 u 是蜡烛到光心的距离，像距 v 是像到光心的距离；轴上的 F 在一倍焦距处、2F 在二倍焦距处，是两个分水岭点。

● u>2f · 缩小实像　● f<u<2f · 放大实像　● u<f · 放大虚像

物距 u 180
远处 3f（u = 180）
恰在 2f（u = 120）
f 与 2f 之间（u = 90）
恰在 f（u = 60）
f 以内（u = 30）

u = 180（大于 2f）：像跑到透镜另一侧，像距 v = 90，放大率 0.5 倍——倒立、缩小、实像。照相机就是把景物放在这一段。

第 3 步 · 光屏与眼睛

实像接得住，虚像只能看

这一步要回答：实像和虚像到底差在哪？情境一：蜡烛固定在 u = 150（f = 60），公式给出像距 v = 100。拖动光屏去「接」它——只有屏正好停在像距处，屏上的烛焰才清晰；偏开就糊（这里模糊的程度是按离焦距离画的示意，不是真实光学模拟）。情境二：把蜡烛挪进 f 以内，看看屏还能不能接到像，再换眼睛来瞧。

情境二 · 放大镜的虚像

结论：实像 = 光线真实交汇，能落到光屏上；虚像 = 反向延长线的交点，只能用眼睛看，屏永远接不到。放大镜用的正是虚像——所以放大镜里的字没法「投」到纸上。

第 5 步 · 终章

把这一页收成三句话

蜡烛还是那支蜡烛，透镜还是那块透镜。能预言像的全部本事，就是两条分水岭加三条光线：

一倍焦距分虚实

u > f：光线真实交汇，成实像，在透镜另一侧；u < f：只有反向延长线交汇，成虚像，和物体同一侧；u = f：光线平行出门，像在无穷远。

二倍焦距分大小

u > 2f 像缩小，u = 2f 像等大，f < u < 2f 像放大。外加一条总规律：实像永远倒立，虚像永远正立。照相机、投影仪、放大镜，无非是把物体放在不同段。

三条光线作图

平行线穿镜过焦点，过心线直行不弯腰，过焦点线出门变平行。任意两条交出像点，第三条自动来会合——画错了，它当场拆穿你。

从一束平行光开始，你已经能预言任何距离上的像：先用 1/v = 1/f − 1/u 算像距，再拿 u 和 f、2f 比一比，正倒大小实虚全落地。照相机、投影仪、放大镜，乃至你眼睛里的晶状体，用的都是这同一条公式。

Step 1 · Three Special Rays

Locating one image point takes only three rays

This step answers: the flame tip emits countless rays — how do we know where its image lands? Trick: draw only three rays with rules — after the lens they are bound to meet again at the image point. You can drag the flame tip (up/down changes the height, left/right the object distance) or use the sliders below. Light the three rays one by one and watch where they meet. Here f = 60, and the image distance is not measured with a ruler — the formula computes it: 1/f = 1/u + 1/v.

Ray 1 · Parallel → through focus
Ray 2 · Through centre → straight
Ray 3 · Through focus → parallel
Object distance u (candle to centre) 120
Object height (flame tip to axis) 30

Ray 1: leaves parallel to the axis, bends at the lens toward the far focus F.

Object distance u = 120; the formula gives image distance v = 120. The lit rays meet exactly there: image height 30 (1× the object height 30, inverted). Any two rays fix the point — the third joins on its own.

Conclusion: these three rays are the whole drawing method. A handy self-check: pick any two rays to fix the meeting point — the third must pass through it automatically. If it misses, the drawing is wrong.

Convex Lens Imaging · Move the Candle, Change the Image

A candle stands before a convex lens: far away, its image is small and upside-down; drag it closer and the image grows; drag it past one special point and the image suddenly jumps to the same side of the lens, upright and magnified. Step 0 · Light through a Lens

Parallel light goes in — the lens gathers it to one point

Known: light travels straight in one medium and bends at an interface (refraction). This step answers one question only: where does a bundle of parallel light go after passing through a convex lens? Two names first: the straight line through the centre of the lens, perpendicular to it, is the principal axis; the centre point of the lens is the optical centre O. Drag the focal-length slider and watch where the rays on the right meet.

Focal length f (focus to optical centre) 60

The parallel light is gathered onto one point of the axis — the focus F: it sits 60 to the right of the optical centre (that distance is the focal length); the 2F point sits at 120. With f = 60: The focus is at an intermediate distance; this drawing compares geometry only.

Conclusion: a convex lens is a converging lens — it gathers parallel light to its focus. Conditions: this page draws the idealised case of a thin lens and rays near the axis; rays near the rim of a real lens deviate slightly (spherical aberration), which this page does not develop.

Step 1 · Three Special Rays

Locating one image point takes only three rays

Question: how do rays from one object point locate an image point? In this paraxial thin-lens model, two independent principal rays suffice. Real images are intersections of outgoing rays; virtual images are intersections of backward extensions. At the focal plane the outgoing rays are parallel and there is no finite image point. Ray 3 · Through focus → parallel

Step 2 · Moving the Candle (the core step)

← Knowledge Index

Junior High
Reflection & Refraction

Light travels straight inside one medium, but at a boundary it turns: it bounces off a mirror with the angle of reflection equal to the angle of incidence, bends as it enters water, and — at too steep an angle — reflects entirely back. Every ray on this page is computed from the real laws before it is drawn. Drag, measure, and see what light actually obeys.

中
EN
0 Mirror bounce
1 Diffuse reflection
2 Bending into water
3 Total reflection
4 The fooled eye

Step 0

Mirror bounce: angle in equals angle out

Question: when light hits a mirror, which way does it go? Two terms first: the normal is the imaginary line perpendicular to the mirror at the point of incidence (the dashed line in the diagram); the angle of incidence is measured between the incoming ray and the normal, and the angle of reflection between the reflected ray and the normal — both are measured from the normal, never from the mirror surface. Drag the light source in the diagram (or use the slider) and watch the two arc readings: however you drag, the angle of reflection always equals the angle of incidence. This holds for smooth, mirror-like surfaces.

Angle of incidence (or drag the source in the diagram)
Incidence 0° (head-on)
Incidence 60°
Reset this step

Angle of incidence = 35.0°, angle of reflection = 35.0° — equal.

Note: angles are measured from the normal. Measured from the mirror surface you would get 90° minus this value — textbooks always use the normal as the reference.

Step 1

Rough surfaces: diffuse reflection obeys the same law

Question: paper is not smooth, so why can we read it — yet never see our face in it? Zoomed in, a rough surface is a crowd of tiny facets tilted every which way, each with its own normal (the imaginary line perpendicular to that facet). A parallel beam lands on them; each ray still reflects with angle out equal to angle in at its own facet — this is diffuse reflection: the law does not fail; the normals point in different directions, so the reflected light scatters. Switch between the three views to compare.

Mirror
Rough surface
Side by side

Mirror: the normal points the same way everywhere, so parallel incoming rays stay parallel after reflecting — that is why a mirror forms a sharp image.

We can see non-luminous objects at all because diffuse reflection sends some of the light into our eyes from almost any viewing position.

Step 2

Bending into water: refraction turns toward the normal

Question: how does an oblique ray change angle when it enters water from air? The normal is perpendicular to the surface at the hit point. Incidence θ₁ and refraction θ₂ are measured from the normal on their respective sides. Drag the source or use the slider with the media fixed. At oblique incidence, the smaller refraction angle turns the ray toward the normal; at normal incidence both angles are0°. Expand the sine relation below to check this same ray.

Angle of incidence, air side (or drag the source)
Incidence 0° (straight in)
Reset this step

Angle of incidence = 40.0°, angle of refraction ≈ 28.9° (computed from Snell's law); the ray bent by 11.1° at the surface.

Refraction angle < incidence angle: entering water, the ray leans toward the normal.

The refractive index n=c/v is vacuum light speed c divided by the phase speed v in the medium; it is dimensionless. This ideal model fixes air at1.00 and water at1.33, with homogeneous, non-absorbing media and no dispersion. It computes ray directions, not travel times or reflected/transmitted energy fractions.

Math connection: can a real refraction angle exist?

Step 3

The other way: water to air, and total internal reflection

Question: when can light in water no longer propagate into air? Both angles are again measured from the normal, perpendicular to the surface. Below the critical angle, oblique rays bend away from the normal; at normal incidence both angles are0°. The incidence that gives refraction90°, the limiting ray along the surface, is the critical angle. Strictly above it, there is no propagating refracted ray in air: the ideal interface totally reflects the light inside water. Try30°, the exact critical preset and60°; predict whether a refracted ray exists before checking.

Critical preset (unrounded)≈48.8°

The critical angle is ≈ 48.8° (computed from arcsin(1/1.33)) — drag past it and see.

This critical angle requires higher incident index n₁ and lower exit index n₂: θc=arcsin(n₂/n₁). Here n₁=1.33 and n₂=1.00. The displayed48.8° is rounded; the preset uses the unrounded value. Arrow keys change0.1°; Home/End select0°/80°; dragging is continuous. Below critical, the faint orange ray is ordinary reflection. Line thickness and colour do not encode energy fractions.

Step 4

The fooled eye: the fish is not where it looks

Question: how deep does the fish appear if we trace the ray reaching the eye backward? Light from the fish refracts at the water surface. This diagram extends the outgoing ray backward to the vertical reference line through the real fish and marks an apparent depth there. Move the eye or its slider to compare depths on that line. This explains a shallower appearance; it is not a full multi-ray virtual-image solution.

Eye position, left–right (or drag the eye in the diagram)

Real depth 3.5 units; it looks like only ≈2.3 units — the fish is lifted by about 1.2 units.

The apparent point stays on the vertical reference line through the fish; only depth is compared, not lateral image motion. Near the overhead, paraxial limit, apparent depth≈real depth/1.33. That ratio is not used at large viewing angles.

40°
50°
80°

Quiz 2 · Light enters water from air at 50°. The angle of refraction is —
smaller (bent toward the normal)
larger (bent away from the normal)
the same — no bend

Quiz 3 · A source under water shines at the surface with an incidence angle of 60° (critical angle ≈48.8°). What happens?
It refracts out, with a larger angle
The refracted ray skims along the surface
Total internal reflection — all of it reflects back

Quiz progress: not started yet.

Finale

Wrap-up: three rules at a boundary
Reflection: equal angles out

Angle of reflection = angle of incidence, both measured from the normal. The smoother the surface, the tidier the reflection; a rough surface only scrambles the normals, not the law.

Refraction: a new medium may change direction

Oblique air-to-water rays bend toward the normal; water-to-air rays bend away below critical. Normal incidence does not bend. Snell’s n₁sinθ₁=n₂sinθ₂ sets direction; n=c/v is dimensionless.

Virtual images: the eye looks back wrongly

The outgoing ray is extended backward to the fish’s vertical line to compare apparent depth. This reference-line illustration is not a full virtual-image solution.

Parallel light goes in — the lens gathers it to one point

Known: light travels straight in one medium and bends at an interface (refraction). This step answers one question only: where does a bundle of parallel light go after passing through a convex lens? Two names first: the straight line through the centre of the lens, perpendicular to it, is the principal axis; the centre point of the lens is the optical centre O. Drag the focal-length slider and watch where the rays on the right meet.

Focal length f (focus to optical centre) 60

The parallel light is gathered onto one point of the axis — the focus F: it sits 60 to the right of the optical centre (that distance is the focal length); the 2F point sits at 120. With f = 60: The focus is at an intermediate distance; this drawing compares geometry only.

Conclusion: a convex lens is a converging lens — it gathers parallel light to its focus. Conditions: this page draws the idealised case of a thin lens and rays near the axis; rays near the rim of a real lens deviate slightly (spherical aberration), which this page does not develop.

Step 1 · Three Special Rays

Locating one image point takes only three rays

Question: how do rays from one object point locate an image point? In this paraxial thin-lens model, two independent principal rays suffice. Real images are intersections of outgoing rays; virtual images are intersections of backward extensions. At the focal plane the outgoing rays are parallel and there is no finite image point. Drag the object or use the sliders and toggle rays. This step fixes f=60; distances and heights use the same arbitrary length unit;1/f=1/u+1/v.

Ray 1 · Parallel → through focus
Ray 2 · Through centre → straight
Ray 3 · Through focus → parallel
Object distance u (candle to centre) 105
Object height (flame tip to axis) 18

Ray 1: leaves parallel to the axis, bends at the lens toward the far focus F.
Ray 2: passes straight through the optical centre, undeviated.
Ray 3: leaves through the near focus F, leaves the lens parallel to the axis.

Object distance u = 105; the formula gives image distance v = 140. The lit rays meet exactly there: absolute image height 24 (≈1.33333× the object height 18, inverted). Any two rays fix the point — the third joins on its own.

The finite image and its full height fit in this drawing.

The third special ray is shown only if its lens-plane intercept is finite and inside the drawing. It is unavailable at u=f; use the first two rays to see parallel output. The lens symbol is not an aperture calculation. Large-angle, marginal and thick-lens behaviour is outside this approximation.

Step 3 · Screen and Eye

A real image can be caught; a virtual one can only be seen

Question: which image can a screen intercept directly? This step uses separate fixed scenes: f=60,H=26; real scene u=150,v=100; virtual scene u=30,v=−60. Move screen p and compare with v. Only the unrounded equality p=v is labelled exactly in focus. Blur and patches are defocus illustrations, not irradiance, diffraction or a physical point-spread calculation. The eye icon indicates viewing direction, not internal-eye imaging.

Scene 1 · Catch a real image
Scene 2 · The magnifier’s virtual image
Screen position (distance from centre) 75.3

The screen is at 75.3; the image distance is 100, off by ≈24.7: the image blurs into a blob (blur drawn schematically). The rays have not met yet (or have met and spread again) — the screen only slices a patch of light. Drag it to 100 and try.

A real image is an actual convergence of outgoing rays and can be intercepted there. A virtual image is an intersection of backward extensions and cannot be intercepted directly at that point. Another optical system could form a further image from the rays; that is not simulated here.

Reflection & Refraction

Light travels straight inside one medium, but at a boundary it turns: it bounces off a mirror with the angle of reflection equal to the angle of incidence, bends as it enters water, and — at too steep an angle — reflects entirely back. Every ray on this page is computed from the real laws before it is drawn. Drag, measure, and see what light actually obeys.

中
EN
0 Mirror bounce
1 Diffuse reflection
2 Bending into water
3 Total reflection
4 The fooled eye

Step 0

Mirror bounce: angle in equals angle out

Question: when light hits a mirror, which way does it go? Two terms first: the normal is the imaginary line perpendicular to the mirror at the point of incidence (the dashed line in the diagram); the angle of incidence is measured between the incoming ray and the normal, and the angle of reflection between the reflected ray and the normal — both are measured from the normal, never from the mirror surface. Drag the light source in the diagram (or use the slider) and watch the two arc readings: however you drag, the angle of reflection always equals the angle of incidence. This holds for smooth, mirror-like surfaces.

Angle of incidence (or drag the source in the diagram)
Incidence 0° (head-on)
Incidence 60°
Reset this step

Angle of incidence = 35.0°, angle of reflection = 35.0° — equal.

Note: angles are measured from the normal. Measured from the mirror surface you would get 90° minus this value — textbooks always use the normal as the reference.

Step 1

Rough surfaces: diffuse reflection obeys the same law

Question: paper is not smooth, so why can we read it — yet never see our face in it? Zoomed in, a rough surface is a crowd of tiny facets tilted every which way, each with its own normal (the imaginary line perpendicular to that facet). A parallel beam lands on them; each ray still reflects with angle out equal to angle in at its own facet — this is diffuse reflection: the law does not fail; the normals point in different directions, so the reflected light scatters. Switch between the three views to compare.

Mirror
Rough surface
Side by side

Mirror: the normal points the same way everywhere, so parallel incoming rays stay parallel after reflecting — that is why a mirror forms a sharp image.

We can see non-luminous objects at all because diffuse reflection sends some of the light into our eyes from almost any viewing position.

Step 2

Bending into water: refraction turns toward the normal

Question: how does an oblique ray change angle when it enters water from air? The normal is perpendicular to the surface at the hit point. Incidence θ₁ and refraction θ₂ are measured from the normal on their respective sides. Drag the source or use the slider with the media fixed. At oblique incidence, the smaller refraction angle turns the ray toward the normal; at normal incidence both angles are0°. Expand the sine relation below to check this same ray.

Angle of incidence, air side (or drag the source)
Incidence 0° (straight in)
Reset this step

Angle of incidence = 40.0°, angle of refraction ≈ 28.9° (computed from Snell's law); the ray bent by 11.1° at the surface.

Refraction angle < incidence angle: entering water, the ray leans toward the normal.

The refractive index n=c/v is vacuum light speed c divided by the phase speed v in the medium; it is dimensionless. This ideal model fixes air at1.00 and water at1.33, with homogeneous, non-absorbing media and no dispersion. It computes ray directions, not travel times or reflected/transmitted energy fractions.

Math connection: can a real refraction angle exist?

Step 3

The other way: water to air, and total internal reflection

Question: when can light in water no longer propagate into air? Both angles are again measured from the normal, perpendicular to the surface. Below the critical angle, oblique rays bend away from the normal; at normal incidence both angles are0°. The incidence that gives refraction90°, the limiting ray along the surface, is the critical angle. Strictly above it, there is no propagating refracted ray in air: the ideal interface totally reflects the light inside water. Try30°, the exact critical preset and60°; predict whether a refracted ray exists before checking.

Angle of incidence, water side (or drag the source)
Incidence 30°
Critical preset (unrounded)≈48.8°
Incidence 60°
Reset this step

Angle of incidence = 30.0°, angle of refraction ≈ 41.7° — larger than the incidence angle; the ray leans away from the normal.

The critical angle is ≈ 48.8° (computed from arcsin(1/1.33)) — drag past it and see.

This critical angle requires higher incident index n₁ and lower exit index n₂: θc=arcsin(n₂/n₁). Here n₁=1.33 and n₂=1.00. The displayed48.8° is rounded; the preset uses the unrounded value. Arrow keys change0.1°; Home/End select0°/80°; dragging is continuous. Below critical, the faint orange ray is ordinary reflection. Line thickness and colour do not encode energy fractions.

Math connection: can a real refraction angle exist?

Step 4

The fooled eye: the fish is not where it looks

Question: how deep does the fish appear if we trace the ray reaching the eye backward? Light from the fish refracts at the water surface. This diagram extends the outgoing ray backward to the vertical reference line through the real fish and marks an apparent depth there. Move the eye or its slider to compare depths on that line. This explains a shallower appearance; it is not a full multi-ray virtual-image solution.

Eye position, left–right (or drag the eye in the diagram)

Real depth 3.5 units; it looks like only ≈2.3 units — the fish is lifted by about 1.2 units.

The apparent point stays on the vertical reference line through the fish; only depth is compared, not lateral image motion. Near the overhead, paraxial limit, apparent depth≈real depth/1.33. That ratio is not used at large viewing angles.

40°
50°
80°

Quiz 2 · Light enters water from air at 50°. The angle of refraction is —
smaller (bent toward the normal)
larger (bent away from the normal)
the same — no bend

Quiz 3 · A source under water shines at the surface with an incidence angle of 60° (critical angle ≈48.8°). What happens?
It refracts out, with a larger angle
The refracted ray skims along the surface
Total internal reflection — all of it reflects back

Quiz progress: not started yet.

Finale

Wrap-up: three rules at a boundary
Reflection: equal angles out

Angle of reflection = angle of incidence, both measured from the normal. The smoother the surface, the tidier the reflection; a rough surface only scrambles the normals, not the law.

Refraction: a new medium may change direction

Oblique air-to-water rays bend toward the normal; water-to-air rays bend away below critical. Normal incidence does not bend. Snell’s n₁sinθ₁=n₂sinθ₂ sets direction; n=c/v is dimensionless.

Virtual images: the eye looks back wrongly

The outgoing ray is extended backward to the fish’s vertical line to compare apparent depth. This reference-line illustration is not a full virtual-image solution.

Convex Lens Imaging · Move the Candle, Change the Image

Three questions on the two watersheds

No formulas — just the pocket rule: one focal length splits real from virtual, two split small from large. The axis diagram below stays available (f = 60).

Q1. A camera lens is a convex lens. The person stands far away (u > 2f). What is the image on the sensor like?

Inverted, smaller, real
Upright, magnified, virtual
Inverted, magnified, real

Tap an option to answer.

From magnified to smaller, still a real image
From smaller to magnified, still an inverted real image
Past some point it flips to an upright virtual image

u > 2f
f < u < 2f

Tap an option to answer.

All three questions ask the same thing: first locate u — beyond 2f, between f and 2f, or inside f — and orientation, size and real/virtual are all decided.

The whole page in three sentences

Same candle, same lens. Everything needed to predict the image is two watersheds plus three rays:

One focal length splits real from virtual

u > f: rays truly meet — a real image on the other side. u < f: only the backward extensions meet — a virtual image on the same side. u = f: the rays leave parallel, the image is at infinity.

Two focal lengths split small from large

u > 2f shrinks, u = 2f matches, f < u < 2f magnifies. Plus one blanket rule: real images are always inverted, virtual images always upright. Cameras, projectors and magnifiers merely park the object in different zones.

The parallel ray bends through the focus, the centre ray walks straight, the through-focus ray leaves parallel. Any two fix the image point; the third arrives on its own — and exposes a wrong drawing on the spot.

Starting from one bundle of parallel light, you can now predict the image at any distance: compute the image distance with 1/v = 1/f − 1/u, then compare u with f and 2f — orientation, size and real-vs-virtual all fall out. Cameras, projectors, magnifying glasses and the lens inside your own eye all run on this one formula.

Step 4

The fooled eye: the fish is not where it looks

Question: how deep does the fish appear if we trace the ray reaching the eye backward? Light from the fish refracts at the water surface. This diagram extends the outgoing ray backward to the vertical reference line through the real fish and marks an apparent depth there. Move the eye or its slider to compare depths on that line. This explains a shallower appearance; it is not a full multi-ray virtual-image solution.

Eye position, left–right (or drag the eye in the diagram)

Real depth 3.5 units; it looks like only ≈2.3 units — the fish is lifted by about 1.2 units.

Finale

Wrap-up: three rules at a boundary
Reflection: equal angles out

Angle of reflection = angle of incidence, both measured from the normal. The smoother the surface, the tidier the reflection; a rough surface only scrambles the normals, not the law.

Refraction: a new medium may change direction

Oblique air-to-water rays bend toward the normal; water-to-air rays bend away below critical. Normal incidence does not bend. Snell’s n₁sinθ₁=n₂sinθ₂ sets direction; n=c/v is dimensionless.

The outgoing ray is extended backward to the fish’s vertical line to compare apparent depth. This reference-line illustration is not a full virtual-image solution.

Step 0 · Light through a Lens

Parallel light goes in — the lens gathers it to one point

Known: light travels straight in one medium and bends at an interface (refraction). This step answers one question only: where does a bundle of parallel light go after passing through a convex lens? Two names first: the straight line through the centre of the lens, perpendicular to it, is the principal axis; the centre point of the lens is the optical centre O. Drag the focal-length slider and watch where the rays on the right meet.

Focal length f (focus to optical centre) 65

The parallel light is gathered onto one point of the axis — the focus F: it sits 65 to the right of the optical centre (that distance is the focal length); the 2F point sits at 130. With f = 65: The focus is at an intermediate distance; this drawing compares geometry only.

Conclusion: a convex lens is a converging lens — it gathers parallel light to its focus. Conditions: this page draws the idealised case of a thin lens and rays near the axis; rays near the rim of a real lens deviate slightly (spherical aberration), which this page does not develop.

物理与电路
初中
凸透镜成像 · 蜡烛远近，像变样

一支蜡烛立在凸透镜前：离得远，像小而倒；拖近一点，像大起来；再拖过一个点，像忽然跳到镜子同一侧、正立放大。变的不是魔法，是两条分水岭：一倍焦距分虚实，二倍焦距分大小。这一页所有的像，都由透镜公式 1/f = 1/u + 1/v 当场算出来——图上画的、嘴里说的，必须是同一个像。

中
EN
0 平行光聚成点
1 三条特殊光线
2 蜡烛远近变像
3 光屏与眼睛

第 0 步 · 光穿过透镜

平行光进门，被透镜收拢到一点

已知：光在同一种介质里沿直线传播，穿过界面会拐弯（折射）。这一步只回答一个问题：一束互相平行的光穿过凸透镜，会往哪里走？先认两个名字：穿过透镜中心、且垂直于镜面的那条直线叫主光轴；透镜的中心点叫光心 O。拖动焦距滑杆，看右侧的光线交点怎样跟着移动。

焦距 f（焦点到光心的距离） 65

平行光被收拢到主光轴上的一点——这就是焦点 F：它在光心右侧 65 处（这段距离就叫焦距）；2F 点在 130 处。现在 f = 65：焦点在中等距离，图只比较几何方向。

结论：凸透镜是会聚透镜——能把平行光会聚到焦点。适用条件：本页画的是薄透镜、靠近主光轴的光线这一理想情形；真实透镜靠边缘的光线会略有偏差（叫球差），本页不展开。

开始探索 ↓

第 1 步 · 三条特殊光线

定位一个像点，只需要三条光线

这一步要回答：如何从物点发出的光确定像点？在本页的薄透镜近轴模型中，两条独立主光线即可定位：实像是出射光线相交，虚像是反向延长线相交；物体恰在焦平面时出射光平行，无有限像点。拖物点或用滑杆，逐条切换主光线。本步固定f=60，距离和高度同用任意长度单位；1/f=1/u+1/v。

线 1 · 平行→过焦点
线 2 · 过光心→不弯腰
线 3 · 过焦点→变平行
物距 u（蜡烛到光心） 215
物高（烛焰顶端到主光轴） 18

线 1：平行于主光轴出发，穿过透镜后拐向另一侧的焦点 F。
线 2：正穿过光心，不偏折、直行到底。
线 3：出发时先穿过近侧焦点 F，穿过透镜后变得与主光轴平行。

物距 u = 215，公式给出像距 v = ≈83.2258。图上亮起的光线交点正好落在那里：像高的绝对值 ≈6.96774（物高 18 的 ≈0.387097 倍，倒立）。任意两条线的交点就能定像，第三条会自动来会合。

当前有限像及其完整高度在绘图区内。

第三条特殊光线只在存在有限透镜面交点且位于绘图区时显示；u=f时它不成立，可用前两条看平行出射。图中透镜是符号，不模拟口径截光。大角度、边缘光线及真实厚透镜不由本图精确预测。

第 2 步 · 蜡烛远近（核心步）

蜡烛一路拖近，像连变五副面孔

这一步只回答：物距u改变时，像距与像的类型怎样变？本步固定会聚薄透镜f=60、实物高H=26；距离同用任意长度单位。光从左向右，物点在x=−u，u>0；v>0是右侧实像，v<0是左侧虚像。带符号放大率M=−v/u，正号为正立、负号为倒立；像尺寸的倍率是|M|。先点u=f预设，再按物距滑杆←/→一次（0.1单位）观察两侧有限像距。

● u>2f · 缩小实像　● f<u<2f · 放大实像　● u<f · 放大虚像

物距 u 59.9
远处 3f（u = 180）
恰在 2f（u = 120）
f 与 2f 之间（u = 90）
恰在 f（u = 60）

u = 59.9（小于 f）：右侧光线散开、不相交，反向延长线在左侧交出像：|v| = ≈35940，尺寸倍率|M|=≈600——正立、放大、虚像。放大镜就是把东西放在这一段。

同一结果：u−f=≈−0.1；带符号v=≈−35940；M=−v/u=≈600；像高hᵢ=MH=≈15600。约定Y向上，长度同单位；M无量纲。

模型：理想会聚薄透镜、近轴、实物、透镜两侧相同介质；f>0。忽略色散、像差、有限口径与衍射。各步骤参数独立，本步f不随第0步焦距滑杆改变。图线不是光传播时间或能量比例。

第 3 步 · 光屏与眼睛

实像接得住，虚像只能看

这一步要回答：屏能直接接到哪一种像？本步另用固定情境：f=60、物高26；实像情境u=150、v=100，虚像情境u=30、v=−60。移动光屏比较p与v；只有p=v的未舍入状态标为恰好合焦。模糊与光斑只是离焦示意，不计算照度、衍射或真实点扩散函数。眼睛图标示观察方向，不求眼内成像。

情境一 · 光屏接实像
情境二 · 放大镜的虚像

第 5 步 · 终章

把这一页收成三句话

蜡烛还是那支蜡烛，透镜还是那块透镜。能预言像的全部本事，就是两条分水岭加三条光线：

一倍焦距分虚实

平行线穿镜过焦点，过心线直行不弯腰，过焦点线出门变平行。任意两条交出像点，第三条自动来会合——画错了，它当场拆穿你。
